2310_00811v1.title: Sparse Backpropagation for MoE Training
2310_00811v1.abstract: One defining characteristic of Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) models is their capacity for conducting sparse computation via expert routing, leading to remarkable scalability. However, backpropagation, the cornerstone of deep learning, requires dense computation, thereby posting challenges in MoE gradient computations. Here, we introduce SparseMixer, a scalable gradient estimator that bridges the gap between backpropagation and sparse expert routing. Unlike typical MoE training which strategically neglects certain gradient terms for the sake of sparse computation and scalability, SparseMixer provides scalable gradient approximations for these terms, enabling reliable gradient estimation in MoE training. Grounded in a numerical ODE framework, SparseMixer harnesses the mid-point method, a second-order ODE solver, to deliver precise gradient approximations with negligible computational overhead. Applying SparseMixer to Switch Transformer on both pre-training and machine translation tasks, SparseMixer showcases considerable performance gain, accelerating training convergence up to 2 times.

2607_16427v1.title: Multi-level context Modeling for consistent expert selection in Mixture-of-Experts
2607_16427v1.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables efficient scaling of Transformer models by routing tokens to a small subset of experts. However, existing routers typically condition expert selection on shallow or isolated token representations, which often produce unstable and semantically inconsistent routing decisions across layers. In this work, we revisit expert selection from a representation perspective and identify context incompleteness as a key bottleneck limiting effective expert specialization. To address this issue, we propose Multi-level Context Fusion MOE (MCF-MOE), a framework that constructs context-aware representations by integrating complementary signals from cross-layer semantic aggregation and local token-level interactions, enabling more informative and consistent expert selection. Experiments on language modeling and understanding benchmarks demonstrate that MCF-MOE consistently improves routing consistency and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines, highlighting the importance of contextual completeness in expert routing. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCFMOE.

2605_17598v1.title: Mixture of Experts for Low-Resource LLMs
2605_17598v1.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient model scaling, yet expert routing behavior across underrepresented languages remains poorly understood. We analyze routing dynamics in two architecturally distinct MoE models -- a pure Transformer (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and a hybrid Mamba-Transformer (Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B) -- using Hebrew as a morphologically rich, low-resource testbed. Both pre-trained models exhibit \emph{deep-layer routing collapse}: usage entropy drops sharply in final layers and tokens concentrate on a narrow expert subset, a pattern largely absent for English. Continual pre-training (CPT) on balanced bilingual data substantially corrects this imbalance, increasing entropy and shifting routing toward shared, language-agnostic experts; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone achieves less complete correction. Extending the analysis to Japanese reveals quantitatively consistent collapse signatures, providing cross-linguistic evidence that the phenomenon is a systematic consequence of pre-training underrepresentation rather than any language-intrinsic property. Routing improvements correlate with consistent downstream benchmark gains, positioning routing entropy and expert specialization as principled diagnostics for multilingual capacity in MoE systems.

2410_18035v1.title: MiLoRA: Efficient Mixture of Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Models Fine-tuning
2410_18035v1.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and its mixture-of-experts (MOE) variants are highly effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods. However, they introduce significant latency in multi-tenant settings due to the LoRA modules and MOE routers added to multiple linear modules in the Transformer layer. To address this issue, we propose Mixture of Low-Rank Adaptation (MiLoRA), a novel and efficient LoRA variant. MiLoRA differs from previous MOE-style LoRA methods by considering each LoRA module as an expert and employing a prompt-aware routing mechanism. This mechanism calculates expert routing results once before generating the first new token and reuses these results for subsequent tokens, reducing latency. Extensive experiments and analysis on commonsense reasoning tasks, math reasoning tasks, and widely used LLM evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that MiLoRA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines with comparable tunable parameter budgets. Additionally, MiLoRA significantly reduces latency in multi-tenant settings compared to previous LoRA-based methods.

2608_15102v2.title: A Declarative-Procedural Perspective on Expert Routing in Bilingual Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
2608_15102v2.abstract: We investigate whether Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models develop linguistically structured expert routing during bilingual language acquisition. Inspired by the Declarative-Procedural framework, we analyze lexical, grammatical, and syntactic processing in a decoder-only English-German MoE Transformer trained under sequential language exposure. We construct a probe-based validation set and extract token-level routing distributions to quantify category-dependent specialisation using mutual information, routing entropy, and Jensen-Shannon distance. The curriculum-trained model exhibits a peak mutual information of 0.1148 at layer 5, indicating category-dependent differences in routing distributions across linguistic categories. Surprisingly, a no-curriculum baseline trained on mixed English-German data shows stronger aggregate specialisation, reaching a peak mutual information of 0.2599 at the same layer. These results suggest that interpretable linguistic organization emerges within MoE routing patterns even without sequential language exposure. A replication at a second training seed shows that the no-curriculum condition's specialisation concentrates on a single language whose identity is seed-dependent, whereas the curriculum consistently yields a stable, language-balanced routing profile; rather than uniformly increasing specialisation, staged bilingual exposure reduces single-language dominance. The official Github repository: https://github.com/Amrit828/DP-Theory-MOE-Interpretability-Research

2503_06184v1.title: Sample-aware Adaptive Structured Pruning for Large Language Models
2503_06184v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved outstanding performance in natural language processing, but enormous model sizes and high computational costs limit their practical deployment. Structured pruning can effectively reduce the resource demands for deployment by removing redundant model parameters. However, the randomly selected calibration data and fixed single importance estimation metrics in existing structured pruning methods lead to degraded performance of pruned models. This study introduces AdaPruner, a sample-aware adaptive structured pruning framework for LLMs, aiming to optimize the calibration data and importance estimation metrics in the structured pruning process. Specifically, AdaPruner effectively removes redundant parameters from LLMs by constructing a structured pruning solution space and then employing Bayesian optimization to adaptively search for the optimal calibration data and importance estimation metrics. Experimental results show that the AdaPruner outperforms existing structured pruning methods on a family of LLMs with varying pruning ratios, demonstrating its applicability and robustness. Remarkably, at a 20\% pruning ratio, the model pruned with AdaPruner maintains 97\% of the performance of the unpruned model.

2502_01705v4.title: Progressive Binarization with Semi-Structured Pruning for LLMs
2502_01705v4.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in natural language processing, but their high computational and memory costs hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices. Binarization represents the most extreme form of quantization, yet binarized models still contain redundancy that can be further removed. Pruning provides a natural way to eliminate such redundancy, but naïve combination with binarization often results in severe performance degradation. In this paper, we propose Progressive Binarization with Semi-Structured Pruning (PBS$^2$P), a novel post-training framework that seamlessly integrates binarization and semi-structured pruning. We first propose Stepwise semi-structured Pruning with Binarization Optimization (SPBO), which progressively introduces sparsity while optimizing binarization parameters to jointly reduce pruning and quantization error, yielding more stable and accurate compression. Additionally, we propose a Coarse-to-Fine Search (CFS) that first allocates pruning ratios and then refines element selection, further enhancing overall performance. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families show that PBS$^2$P consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) binary post-training quantization methods in both perplexity and downstream accuracy. The code and models will be available at https://github.com/XIANGLONGYAN/PBS2P.

2412_11629v1.title: QPruner: Probabilistic Decision Quantization for Structured Pruning in Large Language Models
2412_11629v1.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has significantly advanced various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the resource demands of these models pose substantial challenges. Structured pruning is an effective approach to reducing model size, but it often results in significant accuracy degradation, necessitating parameter updates to adapt. Unfortunately, such fine-tuning requires substantial memory, which limits its applicability. To address these challenges, we introduce quantization into the structured pruning framework to reduce memory consumption during both fine-tuning and inference. However, the combined errors from pruning and quantization increase the difficulty of fine-tuning, requiring a more refined quantization scheme. To this end, we propose QPruner, a novel framework that employs structured pruning to reduce model size, followed by a layer-wise mixed-precision quantization scheme. Quantization precisions are assigned to each layer based on their importance to the target task, and Bayesian optimization is employed to refine precision allocation strategies, ensuring a balance between model accuracy and memory efficiency. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that QPruner significantly outperforms existing methods in memory savings while maintaining or improving model performance.

2505_18232v4.title: Two-Stage Regularization-Based Structured Pruning for LLMs
2505_18232v4.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) is largely hindered by their large number of parameters. Structural pruning has emerged as a promising solution. Prior structured pruning methods directly remove unimportant parameters based on certain metrics, which often causes knowledge loss and necessitates extensive retraining. To overcome this, we introduce a novel pruning method TRSP: Two-Stage Regularization-Based Structured Pruning for LLMs. Specifically, we multiply the output of each transformer layer by an initial learnable weight and iteratively learn these weights by adding their $\ell_1$-norm as a regularization term to the loss function, serving as the first-stage regularization. Subsequently, we apply additional regularization to the difference between the output and input of layers with smaller weights, encouraging the shift of knowledge to the preserved layers. This serves as the second-stage regularization. TRSP retains more knowledge and better preserves model performance than direct parameter elimination. Through extensive experimentation we show that TRSP outperforms strong layer-wise structured pruning methods without requiring retraining. As a layer-wise pruning method, it delivers notable end-to-end acceleration, making it a promising solution for efficient LLM deployment.Code is available at https://github.com/fmk345/TRSP.

2506_18952v2.title: LLMs on a Budget? Say HOLA
2506_18952v2.abstract: Running Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices is constrained by high compute and memory demands posing a barrier for real-time applications in sectors like healthcare, education, and embedded systems. Current solutions such as quantization, pruning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offer only partial optimizations and often compromise on speed or accuracy. We introduce HOLA, an end-to-end optimization framework for efficient LLM deployment. Internally, it leverages Hierarchical Speculative Decoding (HSD) for faster inference without quality loss. Externally, AdaComp-RAG adjusts retrieval complexity based on context needs. Together with LoBi, which blends structured pruning (LoRA) and quantization, HOLA delivers significant gains: 17.6% EMA on GSM8K, 10.5% MCA on ARC, and reduced latency and memory on edge devices like Jetson Nano--proving both scalable and production-ready.

2607_08027v1.title: Structured Pruning of Large Language Models via Power Transformation and Sign-Preserving Score Aggregation with Adaptive Feature Retention
2607_08027v1.abstract: This paper proposes an improved structured pruning method for large language models (LLMs) that addresses key challenges in adapting Adaptive Feature Retention (AFR), an unstructured pruning technique, to structured pruning. When applying AFR to structured pruning, three major problems arise: distribution mismatch between heterogeneous pruning scores, loss of sign information indicating optimization direction consistency, and influence of outliers. To address these issues, we propose a unified approach combining power transformation for nonlinear distribution alignment, sign-preserving score aggregation, and percentile-based outlier removal. Experiments on Llama-3-8B, Vicuna-v1.5-13B, and LLaVA-v1.5-13B demonstrate that our method maintains accuracy comparable to unstructured pruning while achieving practical inference speedup through structured pruning.

2310_00811v1__f01.caption: Figure 1: Training curves of Switch Transformer on WMT’14 En-De.
2310_00811v1__f01.description: Five line plots show training curves for Switch Transformer on WMT'14 En-DE, with Epoch (0–350) on the x-axis and a metric ranging from 3.8 to 5.7 on the y-axis. Subplots compare MoE configurations with 2, 4, 6, 8, and 16 experts. The legend identifies "Switch" (blue dashed) and "Switch + Sparse" variants (orange solid, dashed, dotted). The "Switch" baseline consistently yields higher values than the sparse variants. Performance improves with more experts, dropping from ~5.0 (2 experts) to ~4.0 (16 experts). The solid orange line generally achieves the lowest metric values, reaching approximately 3.9 at epoch 350 for the 16-expert model.

2310_00811v1__f02.caption: Figure 2: Training curves of Switch Transformer on ELECTRA-base training.
2310_00811v1__f02.description: Three line plots display training curves for Switch Transformer variants on ELECTRA-base, comparing "Switch + SparseMixer" (orange solid line) and "Switch" (blue dashed line) across Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) configurations with 2, 4, and 8 experts. The x-axis represents Epoch (ranging from 5 to 30), and the y-axis shows values from 0.24 to 0.36. In all subplots, "Switch + SparseMixer" outperforms "Switch", rising from approximately 0.24 to 0.34 by epoch 30, while the "Switch" curve reaches only about 0.32. This performance gap of roughly 0.02–0.03 is consistent across the different expert counts, with the 8-expert plot showing similar trends over a shorter range of 20 epochs.

2310_00811v1__f03.caption: Figure 3: Comparison between Switch Transformer and Switch Transformer without Scaling.
2310_00811v1__f03.description: Five line plots display training curves for MoE models on WMT'14 En-DE with 2, 4, 6, 8, and 16 experts, comparing "Switch" (dark blue) and "Switch w.o. Scaling" (light blue). The x-axis is Epoch (0–350) and the y-axis ranges from 4.0 to 6.2. Both curves decrease, but "Switch" consistently achieves lower final values. The performance gap widens as expert count increases: at 2 experts, curves overlap near 5.4, while at 16 experts, "Switch" reaches ~4.0 versus ~4.9 for "Switch w.o. Scaling". The unscaled method exhibits instability with spikes in the 6-expert plot around epoch 300.

2310_00811v1__f04.caption: Figure 4: Comparison between SparseMixer and SparseMixer without applying mask to sampling.
2310_00811v1__f04.description: This figure presents five line plots of Training Perplexity (PPL) versus Epoch (0–250) for the WMT14 En-DE dataset, comparing Mixture of Experts (MoE) configurations with 2, 4, 6, 8, and 16 experts. The legend identifies "Switch + SparseMixer" (solid orange line) and "Switch + SparseMixer wo. Mask" (dashed orange line). Across all plots, the masked variant converges faster and reaches lower final PPL (e.g., ~4.1 for 16 experts) compared to the unmasked version (~5.1). The unmasked method consistently yields higher perplexity, with visible training instability spikes in the 6-expert configuration.

2310_00811v1__f05.caption: Figure 5: Comparison between SparseMixer and SparseMixer-2rd .
2310_00811v1__f05.description: Line plots show learning curves for WMT'14 En-DE translation with MoE configurations of 4, 6, and 8 experts. The x-axis is Epoch (0–350) and the y-axis is a decreasing metric ranging from ~4.4 to ~5.9. Comparing "Switch + SparseMixer" (solid orange) and "Switch + SparseMixer-2rd" (dashed orange), the SparseMixer variant consistently achieves lower values. At epoch 350 with 6 experts, SparseMixer reaches ~4.7 while SparseMixer-2rd is ~4.8; with 8 experts, values are ~4.4 and ~4.5 respectively. Increasing experts from 4 to 8 lowers the final metric from ~4.9 to ~4.4.

2607_16427v1__f03.caption: Figure 3: Comparison of model’s inference latency across different sequence length.
2607_16427v1__f03.description: This line plot compares inference latency (ms, log scale) against sequence length (512–4,096) for six models: Dense, SMOE, RMOE, SMOE-Dropout, HyperRouter, and MCF-MOE. All methods show increasing latency as sequence length grows. RMOE consistently exhibits the highest latency, rising from ~2,500 ms at 512 to ~20,000 ms at 4,096. The Dense model has the lowest latency at short sequences (~400 ms at 512) but rises steeply. MCF-MOE maintains lower latency than RMOE and Dense at intermediate lengths (e.g., ~1,000 ms at 1,024). At 4,096, all methods converge to approximately 15,000–20,000 ms.

2607_16427v1__f05.description: Box plot comparing usage entropy distribution by layer for MCF-MOE (blue) and RMOE (green) across layers 0–3. The y-axis shows Entropy Value from 1.0 to 1.7. The syntactic category peaks at E3 and E4 (green to yellow-green, ~0.20–0.21), while E0 has the lowest syntactic allocation (dark purple, ~0.05).

2608_15102v2__f03.caption: Figure 3: Layer-wise expert utilisation across routed layers.
2608_15102v2__f03.description: This grouped bar chart, titled "Expert Usage," plots the probability ("prob", y-axis, 0.0–0.45) of expert utilization for eight experts (x-axis, 0–7) across layers 1, 3, 5, and 7. Layer 1 (light pink) peaks at Expert 3 (~0.45). Layer 3 (mauve) peaks at Expert 4 (~0.33). Layer 5 (dark purple) is dominated by Experts 0 (~0.25) and 1 (~0.24). Layer 7 (black) shows high usage for Experts 2 (~0.39) and 3 (~0.39), plus Expert 5 (~0.27). The data reveals distinct layer-specific routing, with Layer 5 favoring lower-numbered experts (0, 1) and Layer 7 favoring Experts 2, 3, and 5.

2608_15102v2__f04.caption: Figure 4: Routing entropy across routed layers and linguistic categories. Lower entropy indicates more concentrated expert utilisation.
2608_15102v2__f04.description: Routing entropy is plotted as a bar chart across layers 1, 3, 5, and 7 for grammatical, lexical, and syntactic categories. The y-axis shows entropy values from 0.00 to roughly 1.80. Lexical routing (orange bars) shows high entropy, peaking at approximately 1.80 in layer 5. Grammatical routing (blue bars) is lowest in layer 3 (about 1.25) and increases to roughly 1.60 in layer 7. Syntactic entropy (green bars) remains stable between 1.60 and 1.70. Given that lower entropy indicates more concentrated expert utilization, layer 3 grammatical routing is the most concentrated, while lexical routing is generally the most distributed.

2608_15102v2__f05.caption: Figure 5: Evolution of routing-category mutual infor- mation across training epochs for the routed layers.
2608_15102v2__f05.description: This line plot displays mutual information I(R;C) (y-axis, 0.000–0.035) across training epochs 1–16 (x-axis) for four layers. Layer 5 (green) exhibits the highest values, rising to a plateau of ~0.036 at epochs 4–8. Layer 3 (orange) peaks at ~0.030, Layer 1 (blue) at ~0.025, and Layer 7 (red) remains lowest near 0.004. All curves show a sharp decrease starting at epoch 9. By epoch 16, Layer 5 drops to ~0.022, Layer 3 to ~0.014, and Layer 1 to ~0.009.

2503_06184v1__f01.caption: Figure 1: The impact of calibration data and importance es- timation metrics.
2503_06184v1__f01.description: Four bar charts display model performance (y-axis, ~60–80%) across datasets BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and ARC-e. Panel (a) compares calibration data (Random vs. Uniform) using First-order (blue/orange) and Second-order (green/red) Taylor expansion, where Random sampling generally outperforms Uniform on BoolQ. Panel (b) compares importance estimation (First-order vs. Second-order) under Random and Uniform distributions; First-order estimation significantly outperforms Second-order on PIQA in both settings (reaching ~77% and ~74%), while Second-order is slightly better on BoolQ under Uniform distribution.

2503_06184v1__f02.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the AdaPruner Framework.
2503_06184v1__f02.description: This architecture diagram outlines the AdaPruner Framework, where a Transformer Layer containing LayerNorm, Multi-head Self-attention, and Embedding Layers (repeated $L$ times) is pruned (indicated by scissors) to create Pruned LLMs. These models undergo Fine-tuning and Evaluation on Downstream Tasks Wikitext2 and PTB. Results feed into a Bayesian Optimization loop, shown as a Performance versus Solution Space graph, which updates a Shared Pruning Solution Space to guide the iterative pruning process.

2503_06184v1__f03.caption: Figure 3: Average performance of structured pruning on LLa-MA-7B at 20% pruning ratio.
2503_06184v1__f03.description: Line plot comparing average performance of structured pruning methods on LLaMA-7B at 20% pruning ratio. The x-axis lists methods (LLaMA-7B, Magnitude, Vector, LLM-pruner-E1/E2, MoreauPruner, AdaPruner, LoRAShear) and the y-axis is average performance (40–65). A blue star marks the unpruned LLaMA-7B baseline at 63.25. The orange "Pruning w/ tune" line consistently outperforms the blue "Pruning w/o tune" line, rising from 53.59 (Magnitude) to 61.44 (AdaPruner). The untuned line ranges from 42.65 (Magnitude) to 58.99 (AdaPruner). AdaPruner yields the highest pruned score (61.44), closest to the baseline, while LoRAShear achieves 60.63 with tuning.

2503_06184v1__f04.caption: Table 2: Ablation study for optimization of importance estimation metrics, calibration data, and different optimization orders.
2503_06184v1__f04.description: The image shows four plots comparing optimization and pruning. Left plots display "BO-TPE" (top) and "Random optimization" (bottom) convergence, plotting "Performance" (24–40) against "Number of trials" (0–120 and 0–350). "Optimization convergence" (red line) stabilizes near 24–25, while "Optimization examples" (blue stars) scatter; BO-TPE converges in ~120 trials vs ~350 for random. Right plots show "Average performance" (50–63) versus "Method". Top-right compares "Pruning w/ tune" (orange, reaching 60.85 at AdaPruner) and "w/o tune" (blue) against "LLaMA-7B" (62.78). Bottom-right compares "Pruning w/ fine-tuning" (50.71 at AdaPruner) and "w/o fine-tuning" (44.87) against "LLaMA-7B" (63.25) across AdaPruner, LLM-pruner variants, Magnitude, and Wanda.

2503_06184v1__f05.caption: Figure 4: Comparison of Bayesian and stochastic optimiza- tion processes.
2503_06184v1__f05.description: Two scatter plots compare "Optimization convergence" (red line with diamonds) and "Optimization examples" (blue stars) for "BO-TPE" and "Random optimization". The y-axis is "Performance" (24–40) and the x-axis is "Number of trials". In the top "BO-TPE" plot (0–120 trials), the convergence line drops rapidly from ~29 to ~24.5 within 10 trials. In the bottom "Random optimization" plot (0–350 trials), the convergence line takes ~150 trials to reach ~24.5. Both methods converge to a similar performance floor of ~24.5, but BO-TPE is much faster, converging in under 120 trials versus over 350 for random optimization.

2502_01705v4__f01.caption: Figure 1: Perplexity of LLaMA-13B on WikiText2 under different bit-widths across various methods.
2502_01705v4__f01.description: Line plot of LLaMA-13B perplexity (log₁₀ scale) on WikiText2 versus quantization bit-width (16 to 0.5) for RTN, GPTQ, BiLLM, ARB-LLM, STBLLM, and PBS²P. All methods start at 5.68 perplexity at 16 and 8 bits. RTN and GPTQ degrade sharply at 2 bits, reaching 25.53 and 152.31. PBS²P (red) maintains the lowest perplexity at low bit-widths, achieving 6.20 at 0.5 bits (near baseline), outperforming GPTQ (6.85), BiLLM (9.24), ARB-LLM (9.66), and STBLLM (17.22). At 1 bit, PBS²P (9.66) beats ARB-LLM (10.18) and STBLLM (11.33).

2502_01705v4__f02.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our PBS2P framework. Coarse-Stage Search: using the layer importance to assign pruning ratios to each layer. Fine-Stage Search: searching the elements to be pruned based on the Hessian-based metrics. Stepwise semi-structured Pruning with Binarization Optimization: stepwise pruning with optimization of binarized parameters.
2502_01705v4__f02.description: The PBS2P framework diagram outlines a pruning pipeline. Top-right "Layer Importance" bars feed a "Coarse-Stage Search" line plot of "Pruning Ratio" versus "Layers" ($L_0$–$L_{31}$), assigning ratio $R_1$ at layer $L_1$ between bounds $R_{low}$ and $R_{high}$. This guides the "Fine-Stage Search" (top-left), which uses inputs X, W, and a "Hessian Metric" to produce a "Prune Mask Group". The bottom row, "Stepwise semi-structured Pruning with Binarization Optimization," shows a sequence from blocks $B_0$ to $B_4$. Each step combines binarized elements (grey/white squares for +1/-1) with continuous parameters $\alpha$ (blue, $\alpha^{min}$–$\alpha^{max}$) and $\mu$ (purple, $\mu^{min}$–$\mu^{max}$) for iterative optimization.

2502_01705v4__f03.caption: Table 1: Perplexity comparison of RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024), ARB-LLM (Li et al., 2025), STBLLM (Dong et al., 2025), and PBS2P on the LLaMA families. The evaluation results demonstrate the perplexity performance on the Wikitext2 (Merity et al., 2017) dataset across various model sizes.
2502_01705v4__f03.description: This table reports perplexity on Wikitext2 for LLaMA-1 (7B–65B), LLaMA-2 (7B–13B), and LLaMA-3 (8B). Methods compared are FP16, RTN, GPTQ, BiLLM, ARB-LLM, STBLLM, and PBS2P with #Block=128 and W-Bits ranging from 0.55 to 16. FP16 (16-bit) yields the lowest perplexity (3.53–6.14). RTN and GPTQ at 1-bit exceed 100,000 perplexity, whereas 3-bit GPTQ reaches ~4–9. PBS2P (0.55–0.80 bits) outperforms STBLLM at identical bit widths (e.g., 7.36 vs 19.48 for LLaMA-1 7B) and matches 3-bit GPTQ results (e.g., 7.36 vs 8.63).

2502_01705v4__f04.caption: Table 2: Perplexity on the OPT family using Wiki2.
2502_01705v4__f04.description: Table 2 reports perplexity on the OPT family (1.3B, 2.7B, 30B) using the Wiki2 dataset for methods including FP16, RTIN, GPTQ, ARB-LLM, STBLLM, and PBS^2P. Columns compare block sizes (mostly 128) and weight bit-widths (W-Bit 0.55–16). FP16 (16-bit) is the baseline (9.56 at 30B). RTIN with 1–2 bits without block padding yields extremely high perplexity (>10,000). For Block=128, PBS^2P with W-Bit 0.80 achieves the lowest perplexity (23.72, 18.32, 10.50), outperforming STBLLM (11.82 at 30B) and GPTQ (13.04 at 30B with 2-bit). Lower W-Bit generally increases perplexity.

2502_01705v4__f05.caption: Figure 4: BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024), ARB-LLM (Li et al., 2025), and PBS2P performed on the PTB (Marcus et al., 1994)and c4 (Raffel et al., 2020) datasets, mainly on LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-13B, and LLaMA2-7B, and we found that PBS2P at 0.8 bits outperforms other methods.
2502_01705v4__f05.description: The image displays a partial results table and a grouped bar chart comparing BiLLM (1.11 bits), ARB-LLM (1.11 bits), and PBS2P (0.8 bits) on PTB and c4 datasets across LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-13B, and LLaMA2-7B models. The bar chart illustrates a metric where lower values indicate better performance; PBS2P-0.8bits (red bars) consistently outperforms the baselines. For LLaMA2-7B on PTB, BiLLM-1.11bits is 5243.02, ARB-LLM-1.11bits is 389.59, while PBS2P-0.8bits is 67.74. The table lists PBS2P results at 0.80 and 0.55 bits with values from 31.20 to 82.14, though column headers are truncated.

2412_11629v1__f01.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of accuracy and memory usage across different fine-tuning configurations for multiple tasks. The bars represent the accuracy of three different methods (LoRA, LoftQ, LoftQ*) on each task, while the markers indicate the memory usage for each corresponding method.
2412_11629v1__f01.description: This dual-axis chart compares accuracy (left axis, 0–80%) and memory usage (right axis, 22–34 GB) for LoRA, LoftQ, and LoftQ* fine-tuning methods across seven tasks: BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, and OBQA. Accuracy bars show LoftQ often outperforming LoRA (e.g., ~68% vs ~63% on BoolQ), though LoRA leads on WinoGrande (~63%). PIQA reaches the highest accuracy (~76% for all methods), while ARC-c is lowest (~38%). Memory usage lines are flat: LoRA requires ~34 GB, LoftQ* ~24.5 GB, and LoftQ ~21.5 GB, remaining constant across all tasks.

2412_11629v1__f02.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the QPruner framework.
2412_11629v1__f02.description: The diagram illustrates the QPruner framework, combining Mixed-Precision Quantization and Bayesian Optimization. Network layers (layer i through layer i+n) feed into "importance-aware quantization initialization" to produce a bit-width configuration [4bit, 8bit, 4bit, 8bit ... 16bit]. This configuration sets the "init state" (green dot) for the Bayesian Optimization below. The optimization plot shows a function landscape with uncertainty shading, where blue dots mark previous trials. The search starts at the init state and converges to an "optimal trial" (red dot) at a peak, marked by a dashed red line.

2412_11629v1__f03.caption: Figure 3: Pareto-front scatter plots for BoolQ and Wino- Grande with 50 data points. The red points indicate the non-dominated configurations within the Pareto frontier.
2412_11629v1__f03.description: Two Pareto-front scatter plots compare memory (GB) against task scores for BoolQ and WinoGrande. Blue dots denote trials; red dots mark non-dominated "Best Trial" configurations. In plot (a) for BoolQ (Memory: 15.0–18.0 GB, Score: 0.41–0.48), the best trials show BoolQ increasing from ~0.43 at 15.0 GB to ~0.48 at 17.8 GB. In plot (b) for WinoGrande (Memory: 15.5–18.0 GB, Score: 0.525–0.540), performance rises from ~0.525 at 15.4 GB to a peak of ~0.539 at 16.5 GB, with no further improvements in best trials at higher memory usage.

2412_11629v1__f04.caption: Table 3: Zero-shot performance and memory. ‘Bold’ indicates the best performance at each pruning rate. Reported in percentage (%).
2412_11629v1__f04.description: Figure 4 displays five scatter plots mapping Memory (GB) on the x-axis (15.0–18.5 GB) against performance metrics for downstream tasks: ARC-c, ARC-e, HellaSwag, OBQA, and PIQA. Blue dots denote trials, red dots mark the "Best Trial". Y-axis ranges are roughly ARC-c (0.275–0.292), ARC-e (0.425–0.452), HellaSwag (0.444–0.449), OBQA (0.345–0.365), PIQA (0.680–0.690). Best trials cluster around 16.5–17.5 GB, with PIQA reaching ~0.690 and ARC-e ~0.452 at ~16.5 GB.

2412_11629v1__f05.caption: Figure 4: Pareto-front scatter plots for different Downstream Tasks
2412_11629v1__f05.description: This figure presents five scatter plots (a–e) for downstream tasks ARC-c, ARC-e, HellaSwag, OBQA, and PIQA, plotting Memory (GB) on the x-axis (15.5–18.5 GB) against task metrics (ranges visible for ARC-e: 0.425–0.450, OBQA: 0.3450–0.3650, PIQA: 0.680–0.690). Blue dots represent trials, red dots indicate "Best Trial" points on the Pareto front. The plots reveal memory-performance trade-offs: in PIQA (e), optimal points (red) cluster at lower memory (~16.5 GB) with high scores (~0.690), whereas in OBQA (d), higher scores (~0.365) correlate with increased memory usage (~17.0 GB).

2505_18232v4__f01.caption: Figure 1: A comparison between existing layer-wise structured pruning methods and TRSP. Deeper blue layer represents greater performance impact, the taller cylinder represents larger data volume.
2505_18232v4__f01.description: This architecture diagram compares "Previous Layer-wise Pruning" (top) and "TRSP" (bottom). Input "X" (blue stack, deeper blue indicates greater performance impact) and "Data" (cylinder, height indicates volume) feed the pipelines. The top method judges "Transformer Layers" by metrics, prunes them, and retrains to produce a "Final Model". TRSP learns "Layer Weights" to "Regularize" layers containing "Valuable Information" (red circles with 1). It prunes non-essential layers (dashed outlines) to create a "More Compact Model" (dark green blocks) that retains valuable layers. Legend defines red circle 1 as "Valuable Information", X as "Input Data", and scissors as "Prune".

2505_18232v4__f02.caption: Figure 2: Details of layer weight learning and regu- larization. P is the set of prunable layers, identified iteratively using the method in Section 3.2.
2505_18232v4__f02.description: Flowchart illustrating "The Second Stage Regularization" alongside Equation (3) ($\min_{W,y} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{X}) + \lambda_1 \mathbf{1}^T y$ s.t. $-y \le S \le y, y \ge 0$) depicts transformer layer processing. It contrasts a prunable layer $i \in P$ with a non-prunable layer $i+1 \notin P$. For layer $i$, a "Regularize($\mathbf{x}^i_{\text{out}}, \mathbf{x}^i_{\text{in}}$)" block is applied; output $\mathbf{x}^i_{\text{out}}$ is scaled by $S[i]$ and added to residual $\mathbf{x}^i_{\text{in}}$. For layer $i+1$, output $\mathbf{x}^{i+1}_{\text{out}}$ is scaled by $S[i+1]$ and added to residual $\mathbf{x}^{i+1}_{\text{in}}$.

2505_18232v4__f03.caption: Table 2: Throughput (tokens/s) and latency (ms) on OPT-13B and LLaMA2-13B. ‘PPL’ is the perplexity on Wikitext2. ‘PR’ is pruning ratio. ‘TI’ is throughput increase.
2505_18232v4__f03.description: Table 2 compares OPT-13B and LLaMA2-13B (Dense vs. TRSP, 0–50% pruning), where TRSP boosts throughput up to 1.85× and reduces latency to ~209 ms, but raises PPL to 15.38 (OPT) and 11.28 (LLaMA2), dropping accuracy to ~51%. Two plots compare TRSP against ShortGPT, LaCo, Shortened LLaMA, and SLEB. The left plot (PPL vs. Pruning Ratio) shows TRSP (red) has the lowest PPL growth, reaching ~25 at 60% pruning, while SLEB exceeds 60. The right plot (PPL vs. Data Amount) shows competitors' PPL decreasing towards the constant TRSP line (~7.2) at 8000 samples.

2505_18232v4__f04.caption: Figure 3: Perplexity of LLaMA2-7B pruned by five methods under different pruning ratios on WikiText-2.
2505_18232v4__f04.description: A table and line plot evaluate pruning. The table lists PPL and Avg_Acc for OPT-13B and LLaMA2-13B using TRSP at 0–50% PR; for LLaMA2-13B, PPL rises from 4.88 to 11.28. The line plot graphs Perplexity (y-axis, 10–60) versus Pruning Ratio (x-axis, 20–60%) for ShortGPT, LaCo, Shortened LLaMA, SLEB, and TRSP against a Dense baseline (dotted line near PPL=10). TRSP (red) achieves the lowest perplexity (~25 at 60%), beating ShortGPT (~48), LaCo (~55), and Shortened LLaMA (~60), while SLEB (light purple) degrades fastest, exceeding 60 perplexity at 50% pruning.

2505_18232v4__f05.caption: Figure 4: Comparison of perplexity on different calibra- tion datasets at a pruning ratio of 25% on LLaMA2-7B.
2505_18232v4__f05.description: This bar chart compares perplexity for five methods—ShortGPT, LaCo, Shortened LLaMA, SLEB, and TRSP—on LLaMA2-7B at a 25% pruning ratio across calibration datasets Alpaca, WikiText-2, C4, and PTB. TRSP consistently achieves the lowest perplexity, ranging from 6.6 on Alpaca to 11.7 on PTB. SLEB yields the highest perplexity, reaching 15.9 on PTB. Overall perplexity increases with dataset complexity, from roughly 8.5–9.4 on Alpaca to 12.4–15.9 on PTB, with ShortGPT and LaCo falling between the best and worst performers.

2506_18952v2__f01.caption: Figure 1: HOLA architecture.
2506_18952v2__f01.description: This architecture diagram details the HOLA model, comprising a speculative decoding module and a Lo-Bi Optimization block. The top orange-dashed section depicts a "Model" input at a "Low Entropy?" decision node: a "Yes" path leads to "Accept Token" (green check), and "No" to "Verify Token" (red check). The bottom pink-dashed "Lo-Bi Optimization" block contains "LoRA Pruning" connected to "Mixed-Precision Quantization" (with a 12/34 icon). Dotted lines extend rightward from the token steps, and an arrow points into the optimization block.

2607_08027v1__f01.caption: Figure 1: Pruning score aggregation process for structured pruning.
2607_08027v1__f01.description: This architecture diagram details a structured pruning mechanism for a Feed-Forward Network (FFN). Score matrices corresponding to weights $W_{gate}$, $W_{up}$, and $W_{down}$ are averaged and filtered via a "Keep top-k%" operation to produce a binary mask vector (shown as [1, 0, 1, 1]). This mask is applied to the FFN weights $W_{gate}$ and $W_{up}$, indicated by scissors icons that remove specific rows (the second element is set to 0). The pruned weights are then combined for the forward pass.

2607_08027v1__f02.caption: Figure 2: Example distribution of AFR pruning scores showing concentration in the center with extreme outliers at the tails.
2607_08027v1__f02.description: This histogram displays the distribution of AFR pruning scores, plotting "Score" on the x-axis (range approx. -3000 to 10000) against "Count (log)" on a logarithmic y-axis (up to $10^7$). The data is heavily concentrated near zero, with a peak exceeding $10^7$ counts. An inset box reports statistics: mean $\mu=0.0006$, standard deviation $\sigma=2.1616$, minimum -2884.0906, and maximum 9803.4688. While the bulk of the distribution lies between -1000 and 1000, extreme outliers are visible as isolated bars near -2500 and 8000–10000. A red dashed vertical line indicates the value 0.

2607_08027v1__f03.caption: Figure 3: Distribution comparison before and after power transformation (b = 2.7). Left: SNIP score distributions before standardization show how power transformation com- presses the densely clustered low-value region. Right: Distributions after standardization demonstrate improved concentration, with the transformed distribution (orange) exhibit- ing reduced spread in the low-importance region w
2607_08027v1__f03.description: Two histograms compare SNIP score distributions before (blue) and after (orange) a power transformation ($b=2.7$). The left "SNIP Histogram" plots value (0.000–0.035) against frequency (log scale, $10^0$–$10^5$), where the "Before" distribution extends to 0.035 and the "After" distribution is compressed near zero. The right "SNIP_std Histogram" plots value (0–500) against frequency (log scale). The "Before" distribution (blue) spreads up to 500, whereas the transformed "After" distribution (orange) is concentrated below 100, demonstrating reduced spread in the low-importance region.
